subject: history
topicDisplay: Changes in Crime and Punishment in Britain, c.500 to the present day
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In Anglo-Saxon England, which system made a group of households collectively responsible for one another's behaviour?
options: The tithing
The wergild
The Bloody Code
The parish watch
questions.explain: In a tithing, members were responsible for bringing any wrongdoer among them to court, an early form of community policing.

questions.q: In a medieval village a woman shouts that her purse has been stolen and everyone nearby stops work to chase the thief. Which practice is being carried out?
options: The hue and cry
Trial by ordeal
The wergild
The Bloody Code
questions.explain: The hue and cry required everyone who heard the alarm to join the chase to help catch a suspected criminal.

questions.q: Why did Anglo-Saxon and Norman courts use trial by ordeal?
options: To let God decide guilt when human evidence was unclear
To punish criminals as painfully as possible
To raise money for the king through fines
To train young men as soldiers
questions.explain: Trial by ordeal was used when a jury could not reach a verdict, on the belief that God would reveal the truth.

questions.q: The Normans added trial by combat to the justice system. What does this best reflect?
options: The Normans' warrior culture and belief that God favoured the victor
A growing reliance on written evidence in courts
The Church's control over all criminal trials
The decline of royal authority after 1066
questions.explain: Trial by combat let accuser and accused fight, reflecting Norman military values and the idea that God would grant victory to the innocent.

questions.q: What was the Anglo-Saxon 'wergild'?
options: Compensation paid to a victim or their family
A tax paid to the king
A trial overseen by a priest
A group responsible for catching criminals
questions.explain: Wergild ('blood price') was money paid to a victim's family to compensate for injury or death and to limit blood feuds.

questions.q: Which new crime was created by William I's Forest Laws after 1066?
options: Poaching
Heresy
Smuggling
Vagrancy
questions.explain: The Forest Laws made large areas royal hunting ground, so ordinary people hunting there for food were now criminals, or poachers.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why vagrancy increased in the 16th century?
options: Rising population, unemployment and the closure of the monasteries
A fall in taxes on imported goods
The building of new prisons across the country
The introduction of the Bloody Code
questions.explain: Economic change, enclosure, unemployment and the loss of monastery charity forced many to wander in search of work, and they were treated as vagrants.

questions.q: Why was smuggling in the 18th century often regarded as a 'social crime'?
options: Many ordinary people benefited from cheap goods and did not see it as truly wrong
It was only ever committed by wealthy landowners
The government openly encouraged it to raise taxes
It was punished more harshly than murder
questions.explain: High import duties made goods expensive, so communities bought smuggled tea and brandy and rarely reported smugglers.

questions.q: During the Second World War, rationing led many people to buy and sell scarce goods illegally, outside official controls. What is this new crime usually called?
options: Black market trading
Poaching
Heresy
Highway robbery
questions.explain: Wartime rationing created the 'black market', where scarce goods were traded illegally, a crime driven by new social conditions.

questions.q: What name is given to the sharp increase in crimes punishable by death in 18th-century Britain?
options: The Bloody Code
The Forest Laws
The Statute of Labourers
The Riot Act
questions.explain: By around 1800 over 200 offences carried the death penalty under what became known as the Bloody Code.

questions.q: Why did juries in the 18th century sometimes refuse to find defendants guilty under the Bloody Code?
options: They felt the death penalty was too harsh for minor crimes
They were paid a fee to acquit prisoners
They wanted more people transported to Australia
They believed prisons were too comfortable
questions.explain: Many jurors thought hanging was disproportionate for petty theft, so they acquitted or undervalued goods to avoid a death sentence.

questions.q: A court record shows a jury deliberately valuing stolen goods below the amount that carried the death penalty, so the accused escaped hanging. This best illustrates:
options: Jury reluctance to apply the full harshness of the Bloody Code
The success of the new professional police force
The reforms introduced by Elizabeth Fry
The impact of transportation on crime rates
questions.explain: Undervaluing goods, sometimes called 'pious perjury', let juries avoid sending petty thieves to the gallows under the Bloody Code.

questions.q: In which year was the death penalty for murder effectively abolished in Britain?
questions.explain: The Murder (Abolition of Death Penalty) Act 1965 suspended capital punishment for murder, and this was made permanent in 1969.

questions.q: Which of the following was a key reason the government used transportation as a punishment?
options: It removed criminals from Britain while providing a cheaper alternative to execution
It was the only punishment permitted by the Church
It guaranteed that prisoners could never reoffend
It replaced all prisons in Britain
questions.explain: Transportation removed offenders, acted as a deterrent and supplied colonial labour, and was seen as more humane than hanging.

questions.q: Who set up the Bow Street Runners in London in 1749?
options: Henry Fielding
Robert Peel
John Howard
Elizabeth Fry
questions.explain: The magistrate Henry Fielding, later joined by his brother John, organised the Bow Street Runners, an early paid force to catch criminals.

questions.q: In which year was the Metropolitan Police Act passed, creating London's first professional police force?
questions.explain: Home Secretary Robert Peel's Metropolitan Police Act of 1829 established the first professional police force in London.

questions.q: What was the main significance of the 1856 Police Act?
options: It made it compulsory for all counties and boroughs to set up a paid police force
It created the first prison in London
It abolished transportation to Australia
It ended the Bloody Code
questions.explain: Earlier acts allowed forces; the 1856 Act required them everywhere, spreading professional policing across Britain.

questions.q: Which prison reformer wrote 'The State of the Prisons' (1777) after investigating conditions across the country?
options: John Howard
Elizabeth Fry
Robert Peel
Henry Fielding
questions.explain: John Howard's report exposed filthy, disease-ridden gaols and argued for cleaner, better-run prisons.

questions.q: A campaigner in the early 1800s visits Newgate Prison and works to improve the filthy, overcrowded conditions faced by female prisoners and their children. Who is being described?
options: Elizabeth Fry
Elizabeth I
Robert Peel
John Howard
questions.explain: Elizabeth Fry, a Quaker, campaigned from 1813 to improve conditions and provide education for women prisoners at Newgate.

questions.q: What was the aim of the 'separate system' used at Pentonville Prison from 1842?
options: To reform prisoners through isolation, silence and reflection
To force prisoners to work on public building projects
To cut costs by housing many prisoners in one cell
To prepare convicts for transportation to Australia
questions.explain: The separate system kept prisoners apart to prevent them 'corrupting' each other and to encourage penitence and religious reflection.
